1.profile:
Oversharing does not require a hack. It can start with a link that was a little too convenient.

In SharePoint Online, a file can be reachable through site permissions, through a Microsoft 365 group, or through a sharing link. An organization-wide or anonymous link can quietly widen access far beyond the people you had in mind.

That matters more now, because AI assistants like Copilot can surface what a user is able to open.

You do not need a big project to begin. Pick one sensitive site, check who sits in Owners, Members and Visitors, and look at which link types are used for files and folders.

1.page:
Oversharing means content in Microsoft 365 is shared more broadly than intended, for example through organization-wide or anonymous links.

In SharePoint Online, access comes from two layers: site permissions (a Microsoft 365 group or the Owners, Members and Visitors groups) and sharing links for single files and folders. Both can widen access over time.

Because most files shared in Teams are stored in SharePoint, these permissions also decide what Copilot can find for a user.

The article explains the mechanics and gives a short checklist for a first review.

A broad link can undo careful site design, and AI assistants like Copilot can surface whatever a user is able to open.

2.profile:
One entry in a permissions list can make a whole site visible to every internal user: "Everyone except external users".

It is easy to miss because it looks like a harmless group name. But granting it access to a site or library means every internal user in your tenant can reach that content, at whatever level you granted.

That is one reason it deserves a look before you roll out AI assistants like Copilot, which can surface what users can already access.

A practical start: check which sites and libraries contain this claim, and compare that with who actually needs access. Do this review in a pilot area first, and have a way back before you change any permissions.

5.profile:
Old sharing links that nobody remembers creating can be a quiet source of oversharing.

Sharing links accumulate quietly: a file shared with the whole organization for a one-time review, a folder link sent months ago, a link that outlived the project.

A safer cleanup order: start with the broadest scopes, focus on content that is sensitive or heavily shared, pilot on one site, and keep a record of what you changed so you can restore access if someone loses it.

The goal is not to lock everything down. It is to remove access nobody needs while keeping collaboration working.

6.profile:
One broken inheritance rarely hurts. Hundreds of them nobody reviews do.

In SharePoint, a library, folder or file inherits permissions from the site by default. Breaking that inheritance is quick and often well meant: one team needs access to one folder.

The cost shows up later. Every unique permission is an exception someone has to remember, review and clean up. That backlog is what the concept of permission debt describes, and it matters more once tools like Copilot surface whatever a user can technically reach.

The article covers how inheritance works, why breaking it adds up, and which native options you can try first, such as separate sites or sharing links for single items.

Full article: {URL}

When you last needed a folder with different access than its site, did you break inheritance or choose another route?

#Microsoft365 #SharePoint #Governance
6.page:
Breaking permission inheritance in SharePoint is a fast fix with a long tail.

By default, content inherits permissions from the site. Once inheritance is broken, the item has unique permissions that no longer follow site-level changes. Each of these is an exception that needs a review process, or it stays in place long after the original need is gone.

That accumulated backlog of overly broad, inherited or outdated access is what the permission debt concept describes. It tends to stay latent until AI tools such as Copilot surface the data.

The latest article explains the mechanics and lists practical alternatives: separate sites, Microsoft 365 group-based access and sharing links for single files.

Full article: {URL}

6.group:
Question for SharePoint admins and site owners: how do you handle requests for a folder that needs different access than the rest of its site?

The quick answer is to break permission inheritance. The trade-off is that every unique permission becomes an exception to review later, and those exceptions can add up to what is called permission debt.

Alternatives exist: a separate site, a team site connected to a Microsoft 365 group, or sharing links such as Specific people for single items. None fits every case, and the right choice depends on the content and who owns it.

7.profile:
Access rarely becomes a problem in one big mistake. It becomes a problem through hundreds of small, reasonable decisions.

That is permission drift: access slowly diverges from business reality through role changes, leftover groups and exceptions nobody removes.

A useful way to think about it: compare what an identity has been granted with what it actually uses. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management calls this the Permission Creep Index, where a higher score means more unused, excessive permissions.

The counterweight is least privilege: the smallest role, at the smallest scope, for the shortest time that still gets the work done.

The article covers how drift happens, where to look for it and what to do about it, with a reminder to test any cleanup on a pilot first.

Full article: {URL}

#Microsoft365 #SharePoint #Security
7.page:
Permission drift is the gradual divergence of an access model from current business reality. It is rarely caused by one bad decision.

Typical drivers: local decisions, role changes, leftover groups and exceptions that are never removed.

Two concepts help to frame the problem. The Permission Creep Index in Microsoft Entra Permissions Management compares granted permissions with permissions actually used; a higher score means more unused, excessive permissions. Least privilege is the principle of giving an identity the smallest role at the smallest scope for the shortest time that still lets it do its work.

8.profile:
A Microsoft 365 group has no view-only access. That one detail explains why many team sites end up with direct permissions.

If a person should only read a team site, group membership gives them edit rights. The documented route is to add them to the SharePoint Visitors group instead.

A simple rule helps: use groups for people who need access to a whole site, and keep direct permissions and sharing links for real exceptions that you can explain and review later.

The article also covers how permission inheritance and least privilege fit into that rule.

8.page:

That is one of the legitimate exceptions to the rule "manage access through groups". Microsoft Learn recommends managing permissions through the group or team where possible and advises against nested security groups.

A governance tool can show you where the problems are. It cannot decide what your rules should be.

A migration rarely happens on one weekend. The phase in between needs deliberate planning.

Migration coexistence means the old and new environments run side by side and stay linked, so mail and collaboration keep working while users move in batches.
